summary.name: Domain Name System
summary.one_liner: The Domain Name System (DNS) is a hierarchical, distributed naming system that translates human-readable domain names into IP addresses and stores other data about Internet resources.
keywords: dns records a aaaa mx ns cname
use_cases: understanding how domain names resolve to IP addresses
learning DNS record types and caching behavior
troubleshooting DNS delegation and glue records
background on DNS history from HOSTS.TXT to BIND
reference for domain name syntax rules
summary.what_it_does: This Wikipedia article describes the Domain Name System as a protocol and service: a tree-structured namespace split into zones, with authority delegated to authoritative name servers. It explains resolver behavior, including iterative and recursive queries, caching governed by TTL, and glue records. It covers common record types (SOA, A, AAAA, MX, NS, PTR, CNAME) and reverse lookups under in-addr.arpa and ip6.arpa. It also gives history from the ARPANET HOSTS.TXT file through the 1983 specifications and the development of BIND.
notable: Covers the DNS protocol, namespace rules, and resolver mechanics in one reference
Traces history from ARPANET HOSTS.TXT to the 1983 DNS specification and BIND
Explains how caching and TTL cause DNS record changes to propagate slowly
caveats: Describes the protocol in general; it is not a software product to install
Some details, such as the TTL range and resolver override behavior, are stated as typical values rather than fixed rules
